title: STORM
text:
A research collective of Square Management








  in brief
  more
  approach


We develop quantitative methods to measure, monitor and stress-test risk — where it actually hides: in the tails of the distribution.


STORM is the quantitative research collective of Square Management. We develop statistical, econometric and machine-learning methodologies for measuring, monitoring and stress-testing risk.
Our current work focuses on financial risk: credit, model validation, stress testing, climate and geopolitical risk.


01 — The mean is not the risk. We propagate the full conditional distribution, or start from the breaking threshold.
02 — Building blocks, not replacements. Each block plugs into the institution’s already-validated internal model. No redevelopment.

title: Methods and foundations
text:
Research area



The applied areas ask the questions. This one builds the tools — and reserves the right to build them without an immediate application.

title: Methods and foundations
text:
How we approach it
This area exists for a precise reason: the other three share more methods than they share subjects. The same distributional argument serves credit, climate and geopolitics; the same validation question arises wherever a model goes into production. Isolating the methodological core avoids reinventing it area by area — and leaves room for work whose application is not yet written.
Sequential and anytime-valid inference. Validating a risk model is traditionally a one-off exercise: fix a date, test, conclude. Real monitoring is continuous, and looking at the same test repeatedly destroys its guarantee. E-values and test martingales offer an alternative: a statistic that can be consulted at any time, including at a stopping time chosen after the fact, without invalidating type-I error control. Applied to PD calibration monitoring, this changes the nature of the exercise — from an annual photograph to continuous surveillance.
Bayesian methods and validation. The Jeffreys test, adopted by supervisors to validate probability-of-default calibration, is a Bayesian object and deserves to be treated as one. Re-examining it in an explicit frame allows us to say in which portfolio configurations it can be trusted, and in which it should not carry the decision.
Quantiles and tail measures. The at-Risk toolkit — quantile regression, parametric smoothing, analytical back-transformation — is generic machinery of which credit is only one use case. Its multivariate extension is open.
Machine learning, with conditions. Explainability and fairness are not afterthoughts when a model decides on a loan: they are properties internal validation must be able to require and measure. As for recent architectures — Kolmogorov–Arnold networks, for instance — we evaluate them without presupposition: the question is what they bring, or fail to bring, to risk time-series modelling.

title: Geopolitical risk
text:
Research area



The regulator no longer only asks what a geopolitical scenario would cost. It asks which scenario would cost three hundred basis points of CET1.

title: Geopolitical risk
text:
How we approach it
Geopolitical risk has a methodological peculiarity: it does not lend itself to a catalogue. A classical stress test only evaluates the scenarios someone thought to write down, and a combination of shocks dangerous for an institution’s own profile may appear in no list. The ECB’s 2026 thematic exercise acknowledges that limit by asking the question in reverse: identify the geopolitical events capable of eroding CET1 capital by at least three hundred basis points.
We treat that request as an optimisation problem, not a drafting exercise. Reverse stress testing is formulated as a constrained plausibility search: among all scenarios that breach the threshold, retain the one the reference density makes most credible. The resulting breaking point is not the most severe — it is the most probable among the fatal scenarios, and that is precisely what makes it arguable in committee and defensible in validation. The exercise stops being a narrative: it produces a documented, quantified object, together with its neighbourhood of nearby scenarios.
The forward direction inherits the distributional argument. Propagating a geopolitical shock through to a portfolio’s default probabilities requires a macro-financial → credit satellite → mapping chain. There too, transmitting only the mean path understates PD levels and says nothing about the tail. The geopolitical stress test on US credit serves as our proof of concept; the mechanism owes nothing to geopolitics and applies unchanged to climate, monetary or sectoral scenarios.
The measure itself remains. A narrative geopolitical risk index cannot be injected into a risk model. Building a usable measure — stable, interpretable, and whose dynamics genuinely transmit to credit — is a project in its own right, and the one on which demand from institutions is currently strongest.

title: Credit risk
text:
Research area



A bank’s credit engine is known, validated and stable. What it lacks is not a new model: it is the distribution it was never taught to transmit.

title: Credit risk
text:
How we approach it
The architecture of credit stress testing is well established. A macro-financial model propagates the scenario, a credit satellite translates it into portfolio risk, and the Merton–Vasicek mapping — the foundation of the Basel IRB framework — converts a latent systemic factor into a default probability. That chain works, it is documented, and it is already internally validated in most institutions.
The room for improvement is therefore not in the blocks. It is in what the scenario loses while passing through them. In practice the scenario is propagated as a mean path, or as a path assumed known, and the credit mapping is then evaluated along it. As soon as PD is non-linear in credit conditions — and it always is — the mapping applied to the mean gives neither the mean of the PD nor its tail. By convexity the approximation always errs in the same direction: it understates PD levels.
Two consequences, both measurable. The first is a level bias, straight through to provisions and capital: in our application, three-year PDs are understated by 7 to 8 %. The second is an absence: no PD quantile, no expected shortfall, while risk materialises precisely in the tail, which is more reactive than the centre.
Our line of work is to recover that information without replacing anything. The satellite stays the satellite; the mapping stays Merton–Vasicek. What changes is the object propagated: the full conditional distribution of the credit factor rather than its expectation alone.
Validation follows the same logic. Validating a PD calibration means deciding whether an observed gap between predicted and realised defaults is compatible with the model. The Jeffreys test adopted by supervisors deserves re-examination in an explicit Bayesian frame: it is not equally reliable across portfolio configurations. And once monitoring becomes continuous rather than annual, the validity of the test itself must be reconsidered — that is the object of our work on e-values.

title: Climate risk
text:
Research area



Before measuring what a climate scenario does to a portfolio, the hazard must be correctly located, correctly bias-corrected, and its tail must have survived the treatment.

title: Climate risk
text:
How we approach it
The climate risk chain is long: an emissions scenario produces a macro-financial pathway and a field of physical hazards; those hazards strike localised exposures whose vulnerability determines damage; damage translates into losses, higher credit risk and heavier claims. Every link can destroy the information that matters.
Upstream, the data. CMIP6 projections come from global models whose grid cells often exceed a hundred kilometres. At that resolution two sites tens of kilometres apart share the same simulated value, and spatial averaging flattens local peaks. Worse: the models demonstrably understate the magnitude and frequency of extreme events — precisely those that concentrate financial impact. Correcting this means rectifying the shape of the simulated law, not only its level. And a bias correction pursues two distinct objectives, with no guarantee that both are met: aligning the simulated distribution on the reference, and carrying the projected change signal through intact. Between two methods equally well fitted on the historical period, one can cut away a substantial part of the signal at extreme quantiles. That selection point is, in our view, the most underestimated in the whole chain.
Downstream, the measurement. The same distributional argument as in credit risk applies to climate scenarios. Applied to NGFS pathways, the at-Risk approach shows that a scenario is not only more or less severe through its mean, but through the thickness and skewness of its adverse tail: rapid-transition scenarios generate markedly heavier tails in the short run, because of the abruptness of the required adjustments. Two neighbouring mean paths can hide vulnerabilities that differ by a factor of two.
A sovereignty constraint. Bias-corrected projections exist, but are not always freely available. Relying on a third-party provider means recurring cost, dependency and a black-box effect hard to reconcile with the auditability requirements imposed on banks and insurers. Mastering these methods internally is as much about data sovereignty as about being able to justify the set-up to a supervisor.

title: About
text:
The collective



STORM — Scenario-based Testing & Optimization in Risk Modeling — is the quantitative research collective of Square Management.

title: About
text:
What we do
We develop, study and apply statistical, econometric and machine-learning methodologies to problems of decision under uncertainty. Much of our current work originates in financial risk management — credit risk, model validation and monitoring, stress testing, climate and geopolitical risk — but the aim is to produce methods that transfer to other domains.
The collective turns quantitative research into concrete methodological building blocks for institutions’ risk teams. This takes two complementary forms: research papers, submitted to and published in peer-reviewed journals, and technical notes, which carry the same work into practice for modelling, validation and steering teams.

title: About
text:
How we work
Two principles run through everything we do.
The mean is not the risk. Standard practice propagates a scenario along its central path. But risk is not read in the mean: it concentrates in the tails. We propagate the full conditional distribution, or we invert the problem and start from the breaking threshold.
Building blocks, not replacements. Our frameworks are modular by construction. Each block is independent and replaceable by the institution’s already-validated internal model. No redevelopment is asked for: the existing set-up produces more, at the same computational cost.
